newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian committee to take up minister's sex case.
newsitem.headline: Belgian committee to take up minister's sex case.

text.p: A Belgian parliamentary commission is set to decide whether a deputy prime minister should be referred to court over allegations of sex with under-age boys.

The commission, which will meet at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT), must decide whether charges in a report from the Brussels prosecutor-general are grave enough to refer Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo to the Cour de Cassation, the country's highest court.
Di Rupo, 45, does not deny being a homosexual but says he had sex only with consenting adults.
"I repeat for the umpteenth time that I have never been involved in paedophilia. What is happening now to me really seems like political scheming," he told reporters on Tuesday.
Homosexuality is not a crime in Belgium. Sex with children younger than 16 is.
Francophone Socialist Di Rupo is a member of the so-called "core cabinet" of Belgium's centre-left coalition government.

He, the three other deputy prime ministers and Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene form a team of five which effectively governs the country. Their decisions are usually rubber stamped by the full cabinet.
Dehaene's spokeswoman told Reuters on Tuesday his government had ridden out previous crises and would survive this one too.
Most opposition politicians stopped short of calling for Di Rupo's immediate resignation, but said that he should step down if parliament decides to lift his constitutional immunity.
"If parliament refers Di Rupo to the court I do not see how he could remain in office," said Didier Reynders, head of the opposition francophone Liberal party and one of the commission members.
He declined to say when the commission would make its recommendation to the full parliament, adding that this depended entirely on the contents of the judicial report.
The commission's 11 members received a copy of the report Tuesday evening. Belgian radio said they would probably try to reach a decision on Wednesday.
The whole procedure is very similar to the one that brought down Belgian NATO Secretary General Willy Claes last year.
Parliament referred him to the Cour de Cassation over allegations of bribery in an army contract in the late 1980s. He has still not been tried.

The accustion against Di Rupo follows an unconnected scandal of paedophile abduction, sexual abuse and murder that has shaken Belgium to the core since the arrest in mid-August of convicted rapist Marc Dutroux.
Ensuing revelations of police and judicial bungling, incompetence and suggestions of political interference have shattered public confidence in the legal and political system.
"Our regime is out on its feet," francophone green party member Oliver Deleuze told parliament on Tuesday.

Some analysts think that the judiciary's request to hear Di Rupo over child sex allegations could be its way of hitting back at a political world which has been highly critical of the way courts have handled the Dutroux affair.

"It is striking that as soon as the political authorities attack the Brussels court about (the handling of) the Dutroux case, the court strikes back at the world of politics," Ghent University sociology professor John Vincke told Reuters.
